overview.title: Contents (continued): chapters 11-14
overview.main_topic: Contents entries for section 11.3 (pretrained segmentation with Segment Anything), chapter 12 (object detection), chapter 13 (timeseries forecasting) and the first four sections of chapter 14 (text classification).
overview.central_idea: The book finishes its vision chapters with pretrained segmentation and object detection (YOLO from scratch, pretrained RetinaNet), then turns to sequence data: timeseries forecasting with baselines, 1D ConvNets and RNNs, and text preprocessing and set (bag-of-words) models.
overview.importance: This page marks the transition from images to sequences, where recurrent networks and tokenization are introduced.

Find the timeseries baseline, 1D convolution and RNN sections.

summary:
This contents page (printed xi in the header) spans four chapters.

**11.3, Using a pretrained segmentation model (printed 318, PDF p.342):** downloading the Segment Anything Model, how it works, preparing a test image, and prompting the model with a target point or a target box.

**Chapter 12, Object detection (printed 329, PDF p.353):** 12.1 contrasts single-stage and two-stage detectors (two-stage R-CNN detectors vs. single-stage detectors); 12.2 trains a YOLO model from scratch on COCO (downloading COCO, creating the model, readying the data, training); 12.3 uses a pretrained RetinaNet detector.

**Chapter 13, Timeseries forecasting (printed 351, PDF p.375):** kinds of timeseries tasks (13.1); a temperature-forecasting example (13.2) with data preparation, a commonsense non-ML baseline, a basic ML model and a 1D convolutional model; **recurrent neural networks** (13.3) — understanding RNNs, a recurrent layer in Keras, recurrent dropout, stacking recurrent layers and bidirectional RNNs; and going further (13.4).

**Chapter 14, Text classification (printed 381, PDF p.405):** a brief history of NLP (14.1); preparing text data with character, word and subword tokenization (14.2); sets vs. sequences, with the IMDb dataset (14.3); and set models — a bag-of-words model and a bigram model (14.4). Section 14.5 (sequence models) continues on the next page.

Pattern to notice: as in chapters 8 and 11, chapter 12 trains a model from scratch and then uses a pretrained one; chapter 13 again insists on beating a non-ML baseline first.

deeper.title: Using printed vs. PDF page numbers
deeper.body: The numbers in this table of contents are the book's printed page numbers. This companion links by PDF page number. For the main body of the book, **PDF page = printed page + 24** (for example, chapter 12 starts on printed page 329, which is PDF p.353; chapter 14 on printed 381, PDF p.405). The offset was checked against the chapter-opener pages; it is a property of this PDF, not something the book states.

misconceptions.claim: The page numbers in the contents are the PDF page numbers.
misconceptions.correction: They are printed page numbers. In this PDF the main body is offset by 24 pages (e.g. printed 16 = PDF p.40).

later.note: 12.2 training a YOLO model from scratch.

takeaways: Chapter 12 contrasts two-stage (R-CNN) and single-stage detectors, trains YOLO from scratch and uses a pretrained RetinaNet.
Chapter 13 introduces RNNs after a non-ML baseline, a basic model and a 1D ConvNet.
Chapter 14 starts with tokenization (character, word, subword) and order-free set models.

questions.explanation: 12.2 is 'Training a YOLO model from scratch'. RetinaNet is used pretrained (12.3), R-CNN is discussed as the two-stage family (12.1), and SAM is a segmentation model (11.3).

questions.question: What two prompt types are used with the Segment Anything Model?
questions.answer: A target point and a target box.

questions.question: Why does the temperature-forecasting example start with a commonsense, non-ML baseline?
questions.answer: To know what level of performance a trivial method achieves, so that any ML model's improvement can be judged meaningfully.
